title: A day of resolve
hookLine: do the thing you've been putting off
tomorrow: why picture a mother's love for one child to mean love for all?

lines: THE LINE THAT NEVER GETS CROSSED OFF.
cards: Every to-do list has one line that never gets crossed off. Call the dentist. Write the email.
Every morning it slides to tomorrow. Here's a scene about tomorrow. A grove near Kusinara, between two sala trees.
The Buddha is lying on his right side, and he is dying. The monks have gathered close. He asks them whether anyone still has a doubt, a question they've been meaning to ask.
Ask now, he says, so you won't be sorry later that your teacher was right here and you said nothing. Nobody speaks. Then he says the last thing he'll ever say.

teach.b: Here they are, in Rhys Davids' old translation: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" Two sentences, and they lean on each other. The first is the reason.
The second is the job. Everything put together comes apart: the body, the plan, the free afternoon. So the work can't wait for a better week.
The Pali word under diligence is appamada: heedfulness, not letting things slide. Not panic, and not a grind. Just not sleeping through it.

A sutta in the Majjhima Nikaya says it even more plainly: do today's work with energy, because who knows, death may come tomorrow, and there's no bargain to strike with it. That line isn't there to frighten anyone.
It's there to shrink the gap between knowing and doing. And look at the scene again.
Before his last words, he asked for questions. He gave everyone one more chance to say the thing they'd been putting off saying. So a day of resolve isn't a day of doing everything.
It's a day of doing the one thing. The email. The apology.
The first page. Yesterday, resolve lived in a heart.

how: Vesak, which Theravada Buddhists keep in memory of the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing, is one time his last words on heedfulness (appamada) are recalled and taught.

games.q: what does “a day of resolve” mean?
o: the day a promise gets a date: today
a day of waiting until the mood is right
a day for planning big goals for the year

games.q: the last scene — tap the pairs.
p: he asked if anyone had a question

s: resolve means waiting until you feel ready
the last words tie the job to now: things come apart, so don't let it slide.
before his last words, the Buddha asked the monks for any last questions
ask now, he said, so you won't be sorry later. nobody spoke.
diligence here means grinding until you burn out
appamada is heedfulness: not sleeping through it. not panic, not a grind.

games.q: the group project is due friday and your part, the slides, has been sliding all week. it's tuesday night. what fits a day of resolve?
o: pull an all-nighter and finish every slide, to prove you mean it.
open the file and make the first slide, tonight.
wait for thursday. you work better under pressure anyway.
games.why: appamada is heedfulness, not a grind. the one thing, started today, is resolve with a date on it.

practice: Sit easy and let the one thing you've been putting off come to mind. Don't solve it. Shrink it: find the very first move, small enough to take five minutes, and see yourself making it right after this sit.

wordCard.voice: A day of resolve: the day a promise gets a date, and the date is today. Appamada, heedfulness, is what keeps it.

orig.note: Pali: heedfulness, not being careless; the word behind 'with diligence' in the Buddha's last words.

carryVoice: Keep this one: today, not someday, the job the last words gave. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta 6.10 (the last words)
